tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the peer-reviewed ASPLOS 2024 paper (Yedidia, 'Lightweight Fault Isolation', Table 4 and Figure 4) measures LFI against WAMR 1.2.2 AOT, Wasm2c 1.0.33 and Wasmtime 16.0.0 AOT on SPEC CPU2017 with LLVM 15.0.7 on Apple M1 and GCP T2A, with an artifact (zyedidia/lfi-artifact). Not A because SPEC CPU2017 sources are licensed rather than public and the compile flags live only in the artifact's SPEC config files, not in the paper.

corrections.baseline: WebAssembly ahead-of-time engines: WAMR 1.2.2 (LLVM AOT), Wasm2c 1.0.33 + Clang (with UVWASI), Wasmtime 16.0.0 (Cranelift AOT); all relative to native code compiled with LTO
corrections.claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2024 paper Table 4, geomean run-time overhead over native LTO code on the 7 SPEC CPU2017 rate benchmarks that build for WASI: LFI 7.3% (GCP T2A) / 6.4% (Apple M1) vs WAMR 22.3% / 18.2%, Wasm2c 40.7% / 37.5% (16.5% / 15.7% after the paper's barrier removal and pinned heap register), Wasmtime 47.0% / 67.1%. Derived from page data: LFI-sandboxed code runs about 1.14x (T2A) / 1.11x (M1) faster than WAMR AOT, about 1.09x faster than the tuned Wasm2c, and 1.37x / 1.57x faster than Wasmtime. Over all 14 supported SPEC benchmarks LFI O2 overhead is 6.4% (M1) and 7.3% (T2A), about 1% when loads are not sandboxed. Repo README at HEAD: 7% (Arm64) / 8% (x86-64) overhead for read and write sandboxing, 1.5% / 6% for writes only (geomean SPEC 2017); lfi-research README: LLVM-based AOT Wasm compilers 'incur upwards of 20% runtime overhead'.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: LLVM/Clang 15.0.7 with the LFI rewriter for native, LFI and Wasm builds; Wasm bytecode further optimized with wasm-opt, SIMD128 enabled, bounds checks replaced by guard pages; Wasmtime run in AOT mode. Per-benchmark SPEC compile flags are in the artifact's cpu2017/config files (paper text does not list them; artifact not opened).
corrections.hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Air 3.2 GHz (Asahi Linux 6.3.0); Google Cloud T2A instance 3.0 GHz (Linux 6.1.0)
corrections.workload: Run-time overhead versus native code compiled with LTO on SPEC CPU2017 single-copy rate C/C++ benchmarks (14 for LFI; the 7 that build under WASI for the Wasm comparison), Arm64 only in the paper, for in-process software sandboxing compared with WebAssembly AOT sandboxing.
corrections.caveats: Different execution model from a Wasm VM: LFI sandboxes native code recompiled with its own LLVM toolchain and replaces Wasm rather than running Wasm faster. Paper numbers are Arm64 only and were measured on the original research implementation (lfi-research branch, MPL-2.0; repo HEAD is MIT and the code now lives in sibling repos lfi-runtime, lfi-rewriter, lfi-verifier after submodules were removed in January 2026). The x86-64 figures (8% and 6%) in the HEAD README have no linked measurement; the lfi-research README gave ~9-10% for x86-64. In the paper WAMR and the modified Wasm2c were run as non-conforming Wasm implementations (no trap-semantics compiler barrier), only 7 of 14 benchmarks could be compared with Wasm, and SPEC CPU2017 is a licensed suite so reproduction needs a SPEC licence (artifact offers CoreMark as an alternative). Research project; x86-64 verifier was incomplete in the research version.

notes: Paper read from the raw.githubusercontent.com mirror of zyedidia/zyedidia.github.io (the github.io page itself is blocked); Table 4 confirms LFI's 6-7% overhead vs 15-67% for WAMR, Wasm2c and Wasmtime, so the record's search-snippet figures (Wasmtime about 150%, wasm2c about 197%) were wrong and are replaced. Tier raised C to B on the peer-reviewed paper; baseline now named (WAMR and Wasmtime are category baselines). Metadata checked: MIT at HEAD (MPL-2.0 on lfi-research), 119 stars, last commit 2026-01-27, active.

tier_reason: First-party CoreMark table in the README with CPU models and a public harness (coremark/src/main.rs, cargo run --release), but no rustc or C compiler version, and the wasm3 path is commented out of the harness at HEAD, so the Wasm3 column cannot be reproduced as published. Independent wasmi-benchmarks plots exist but measure a bug-fixed fork (Robbepop/stitch v0.1-dev), not this repo, so they do not lift this entry to B.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release in coremark/ (Rust release profile; rustc version not stated). Harness pins wasmi 0.31.2 and wasmtime 20.0.1; the wasm3 runner (wasm3 crate 0.3.1) is commented out in coremark/Cargo.toml and coremark/src/main.rs at HEAD.
corrections.caveats: Only a single CoreMark workload; the edge over wasm3 is within a few percent on Mac and negative on Linux, and Wasmtime's JIT is 4-8x faster than Stitch, so it does not beat any JIT baseline in the category. The Wasmi baseline is the old 0.31.2 stack interpreter (open issue #2 asks for an update since Wasmi 0.32+ is much faster); the wasm3 runner is commented out of the published harness. Open correctness issues #3 and #4 (filed by the Wasmi author, July 2025 and June 2026): live locals and registers are not preserved on entering block/if/loop, so some modules return wrong results (example returns 0 instead of 42); unfixed upstream. Relies on LLVM sibling-call optimisation with no guarantee; 64-bit only; no SIMD or WASI; large amount of unaudited unsafe code (README). Independent wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks plots (Aug 2026; criterion, profile.bench lto=fat, codegen-units=1) measure a bug-fixed fork (Robbepop/stitch branch v0.1-dev, shown as 'Stitch (lazy)'): geomean execute time relative to the fastest runtime is Stitch 15.73 vs Wasm3 (eager) 16.51 on AMD EPYC 7763, 11.94 vs 12.64 on Apple M2 Pro, 9.70 vs 10.71 on Apple M4 Pro (about 1.05-1.10x faster than Wasm3, derived from page data), but Wasmi v2 (eager) is faster than Stitch on all three (12.40, 8.83, 8.06). The record's claim about rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark was not checked by the verifier.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (2950/1684/4592 vs Wasm3 2911/1734/3951; Windows about 1.16x, derived). Keep at C; shortcomings to record: wasm3 runner commented out of the harness, stale Wasmi 0.31.2 baseline, unfixed wrong-result bugs (issues #3, #4), Wasmi v2 now faster in the independent wasmi-benchmarks suite. Metadata checked: MIT, 144 stars, last commit 2025-11-20, active.

tier_reason: First-party doc with public harness (scripts/bench_jit_coldstart.py at HEAD), build flags (-Djit=true -Doptimize=fast) and CPU model (AMD EPYC 9V74, 8 vCPU Azure VM), but the Zig compiler version and the wasmtime version are not stated, so not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: zig build -Djit=true -Doptimize=fast (ReleaseFast) via scripts/bench_jit_coldstart.py, measured at PR-branch commit 329c29b5 whose build.zig.zon requires Zig >= 0.16.0 (HEAD now requires the signed cataggar/zig 0.17.0); wasmtime taken from ~/.wasmtime/bin with no version stated.
corrections.caveats: Cold-start win is on a trivial 36-byte no-op module where wasmtime's fixed per-invocation cost dominates (process spawn included, 20 samples after 3 warmups); the doc itself says wasmtime is about 2.1x faster on CoreMark steady state (3 runs per mode). No comparison against upstream C WAMR, the project this ports to Zig, so it does not show being faster than its origin. Benchmarked with ReleaseFast while the README recommends ReleaseSafe builds. Single x86_64 host, no aarch64 numbers; wasmtime and Zig versions not stated in the doc. Small fork maintained with AI assistance (every recent commit co-authored with GitHub Copilot); 5 stars.

notes: Bench doc numbers match the record exactly (JIT .fast 1.430 ms vs wasmtime run 6.964 ms cold start, about 4.9x; CoreMark wasmtime 26,462.6 vs AOT 12,442.8 iter/s). Shortcomings to record: startup-only win on a no-op module, about 2.1x slower than wasmtime on throughput, no upstream-WAMR comparison, tool versions unstated. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, fork of bytecodealliance/wasm-micro-runtime, 5 stars, last commit 2026-10-05, active.
